en: The Secret Essential Method of the Tripiṭaka,
translated by Amogha by Imperial Decree:
With both hands joined in the ordinary *añjali* at the level of the chest, the mantra is as follows:
This divine mantra is inconceivable; after no more than seven recitations, all that is sought shall be definitively fulfilled and perfected.
Furthermore, it severs the fundamental ignorance of the first stage and leads one to the rank of wondrous enlightenment.

For all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whatever various divine mantras and dharmas they uphold, if there are instances where *siddhi* has not been achieved, those who practice this dharma will find that all such [obstacles] are entirely [overcome].
Next, the method for establishing the mandala by painting images is explained: one should quickly achieve and obtain [the state].

Furthermore, regarding the construction of the threefold inner court, the King of Passion (Rāgarāja) has four faces, each with five eyes—meaning one eye on the forehead, two original eyes on the left and right, and one eye below each;
he wears a jeweled crown, his hair blazes like flames, and his body is white in color.
He is light blue in color and has four arms. His left upper hand holds a bow above his head, and his right upper hand holds an arrow at his chest in the posture of shooting at the Seven Stars.
His two lower hands are positioned to seize the opponent; his right lower hand holds a white lotus and strikes the opponent.
He has four legs: his two left legs are placed upon [the opponent], while his two right legs hang down, treading into the earth.
The Lotus [deity] sits upon a white lotus flower resting on a sun disc; beneath that seat are four-faced lions with four legs, each treading upon a snake.
From the mouths of these lions, wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*) rain down. In the middle court of the upper tier, there are two-headed *Rāgarati* Bodhisattvas;
their forms have two heads, one white on the left and one red on the right, and they possess four arms, with one hand on each side.
Forming the sword mudrā, then with both hands holding three crescent-shaped spears (*triśūla*), seated upon a red lotus and abiding within a sun disc—this is named the Eastern Host.

Furthermore, there is the Bodhisattva Ten Thousand Loves; his form has three faces and three eyes, his flesh is soft and white in color, and he sits with palms joined upon a white lotus, abiding within a sun disc—this is the Southern Host. Furthermore, there is the Bodhisattva Ten Thousand Loves...
Sakki is red-black in color with one face, holding a bow and arrow; he sits upon a yellow lotus and dwells within a solar disc.
He is named the Lord of the West for his assembly. Furthermore, there is the Bodhisattva Sarvaguṇa, whose form is like that of Śrī-devī;
he holds skulls in his left and right hands, sits upon a purple lotus, and dwells within a solar disc. He is named the Lord of the North for his assembly. The Great Heavenly Kings have four corners.
Regarding the Eastern-Southern corner, there is the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra;

his form is blue, he has three faces like a yakṣa king, he wears armor, and he has four arms—the left upper hand holds a bell and the right upper hand holds a sword, while the two lower hands are joined in *añjali*;
he rides a blue dragon. Regarding the Southwestern corner, there is the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka; his form is red.
He has four faces and three eyes, his body like that of a yakṣa king as described before, and six arms: the left upper hand holds a sword and the right a spear;
the two middle hands hold snakes; the two lower hands hold clubs; and the two lowest hands are joined in *añjali* with the palms hanging down, mounted upon a red dragon.
In the northwest corner is King Vairocana, white in form, with one face, wearing armor, and having three eyes and four [arms].

In each hand he holds a sword; his body is as described before, riding upon a white dragon. In the northeast corner is Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, black in color, with one face and ten arms, according to the *Hūṃkāra* ritual.
In the third enclosure, the four types of gathering (*saṃgraha*) and the eight offering Bodhisattvas should be painted as usual.
Furthermore, this is the final secret ritual of all these methods; it must not be transmitted to those who are not disciples.

My son, you must strive and strive; this may not be transmitted to others. If it were transmitted, the Dharma-essence would be lost, and one would incur disaster and receive the karmic retribution of great poverty.
In future lives, one will surely fall into the city of Avīci Hell. Therefore, serve the Master with all your strength;
you must certainly receive it and you must certainly attain it. This painted scroll—if it is not obtained—will be of no benefit for two lifetimes.
The sequential ritual procedures are as in the *Ākāśagarbha-dhāraṇī* method; they are vast and inconceivable, and one should not give rise to doubt regarding these ritual methods.
Transcribed by the master [of the manuscript], transmitted and personally received by Xuan.
The monk-superintendent (Sōjō) Seikai of Jizōin held the original manuscript written by the hand of the monk-superintendent (Sōjō) Seijō of Henchiin;
it was subsequently lent for transcription, and thus this copy was hastily transcribed and retained.
It includes the mandala paper and the iconographic forms, and judging by these, it appears to have been transcribed [from the original].
At that time, in the latter half of the nineteenth year of Eikyō,
the old companion from Saigoku, Ryūgen.
